rationale: The entry's core unifies Prov 30:33's churning mechanic, Isa 7:15's explicit purpose clause (eat butter... know to refuse evil and choose good), the remnant diet of Isa 7:22, Job 29:6's washing of steps, and Ps 55:21's smoother-than-butter speech under one referent (worked milk-word becoming tested discernment, with a walk-cleansing application and a counterfeit). The common abundance reading leaves these as disconnected poetic or literal uses and cannot explain why butter-eating is teleologically tied to moral discernment or why steps are washed with it. Once milk = word is granted by the supplied method, the texts carry the entry better than any rival.
book_core_identification: Butter is milk (the word) churned/worked into sound judgment—teaching tested until one can refuse evil and choose good.
book_secondary_elaborations: Worked into the walk, it cleanses the feet
Its counterfeit is smooth speech concealing war
chapter_only_objections: Jael's water-milk-butter escalation as a full symbolic ladder
Abraham's table and Deut 32:14 as divine acceptance of the symbol
Explicit equation of the rock's oil with pressed works beside butter
strongest_counter_interpretation: Butter/curds primarily denotes rich pastoral abundance, prosperity, and divine material provision (often paired with honey or oil); Isa 7:15–22 is either a sign of post-judgment subsistence or the ordinary diet of a growing child reaching the age of moral choice; Job 29:6 is hyperbolic prosperity; Ps 55:21 is an independent simile for flattery; no unified technical symbol for ‘worked word’ is required.
counter_core_identification: Butter symbolizes abundance, prosperity, and the fatness/rich provision of the land or of hospitality.
material_core_denial: The texts do not identify butter as the word worked into sound judgment; Isa 7:15's purpose clause concerns natural maturation or a reduced diet, not a technical figure for tested teaching derived from milk.
counter_case: Deut 32:13–14, Job 20:17, Job 29:6, 2 Sam 17:29 and Gen 18:8 treat butter/curds as concrete rich food of blessing or hospitality.
Isa 7:21–22 places butter in a depopulated land after agricultural collapse, supporting scarcity rather than matured doctrine.
Ps 55:21 is a one-off simile for hypocritical speech, not the counterfeit of a doctrinal symbol.
No verse explicitly equates butter with ‘sound judgment’ or ‘teaching tested’; the link requires importing milk = word and Heb 5:14.
John 13 concerns water, not butter, so the feet-cleansing claim is an extra-textual bridge.
book_explanatory_advantages: Prov 30:33 supplies an explicit production mechanic (churning milk yields butter) that maps directly onto working the milk-word.

Isa 7:15's purpose clause (‘that he may know to refuse the evil and choose the good’) matches the exact discernment language of mature teaching (Heb 5:14) and is otherwise left dangling by abundance or subsistence readings.
Job 29:6's non-literal ‘washed my steps with butter’ is explained as the worked word cleansing the walk, cohering with the feet-washing register of John 13.
Ps 55:21's ‘smoother than butter... war in his heart’ is explained as the counterfeit of the same symbol, preserving structural consistency rather than an isolated metaphor.
Isa 7:22's remnant eating butter from abundant milk becomes the worked product of the received word, unifying the chapter's diet texts.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Fits the majority of literal and poetic dairy contexts without requiring a prior milk = word premise.
Accounts for the hospitality scenes (Gen 18, Judg 5, 2 Sam 17) as simple rich provision.
unresolved_objections: The precise degree to which John 13 water-washing must be read as the same cleansing performed by butter remains an analogical step rather than a direct lexical identity.
